title: Knowing
description: Say what you know, and what you remember.
grammarNote: Saber is for facts, conocer is for people and places: sé la respuesta, conozco Madrid.

explanation.summary: Spanish splits to know into two verbs. Saber is for facts and for how well you know something. Conocer is for people, places and things you get to know.

sections.heading: Saber and conocer
sections.body: Saber is for a fact: sé la respuesta, no sé su nombre, sabes español. Conocer is for a person or a place: conozco a Ana, conozco Madrid, no conozco esta canción. When you meet someone, you use conocer. When you learn a fact, you use saber.

examples.en: Do you know where the hotel is?
I do not know his phone number.

sections.heading: The forms
sections.body: Saber is irregular in the yo form: sé, sé, sabe, sabemos, sabéis, saben. Conocer is regular except for the yo form: conozco, conoces, conoce. Both verbs take a direct object: sé la respuesta, no conozco el restaurante.

sections.heading: When they come together
sections.body: You can use either, and the meaning changes. Conocer means to be acquainted with: conozco a Pedro. Saber means to know about, which is deeper: sé todo sobre Pedro. And after saber, a following word goes in the sentence with an article: sé la contraseña, but sé español without one.

items.note: For facts. Its forms are irregular: sé, sabes, sabe.
For people and places. Its yo form is conozco.
An infinitive ending in -ar: recuerdo, recuerdas, recuerda.
An infinitive ending in -ar: olvido, olvidas, olvida.
An infinitive ending in -er: entiendo, entiendes, entiende.
Masculine: el idioma. A particular language takes its own name: el español.
